newsitem.title: FRANCE: Juppe says France is even-handed in Mideast.
newsitem.headline: Juppe says France is even-handed in Mideast.

text.p: Prime Minister Alain Juppe insisted to leaders of France's Jewish community on Saturday that Paris was not biased in favour of the Arab stance in the Middle East conflict.

"French positions are not always well understood and there have been accusations, which you have just echoed, that our policy is balanced in favour of one side (the Arabs) rather than the other," Juppe said.

"But that is not the case. France's only bias is in favour of peace," Juppe said at a traditional annual banquet at which serving prime ministers address leaders of the 750,000-strong Jewish community.

Juppe had just heard Henri Hajdenberg, president of CRIF, the umbrella body for French Jewish groups, tell him, and several hundred other guests, that France's Mideast policy was "unbalanced...incomprehensible and clumsy".
"I regret to say that (official) France seems to give the impression it has chosen its camp," Hajdenberg said.

He singled out President Jacques Chirac's conduct during a Middle East tour in October when he publicly clashed with Israeli officials in Jerusalem and made no mention of the heavy presence of Syrian forces in Lebanon when visiting there.
Juppe replied that France's preoccupations included "our attachment to the security of our friend Israel".

He added, however, that France backed the right of self-determination for Palestinians and the principle of exchanging land for peace which rightist Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu frowns upon.
"If we sometimes seem to demand so much from Israel, it is because Israel is so close to us," Juppe said.
Commentators noted that, with crucial general elections just over a year away, Juppe was accompanied by half a dozen cabinet ministers, including Foreign Minister Herve de Charette.

Lionel Jospin, head of the opposition Socialist Party, now favoured to win the elections, was also present as was Robert Hue, new reformist Communist party chief. It was the first time a Communist leader had attended after years of hostility to Israel.

Juppe assured appreciative listeners that his Gaullist Rally for the Republic (RPR) party would ban its candidates from any election-time alliance, even tacit, with Jean-Marie Le Pen's extreme-rightist National Front party, bogeyman to French Jews.

In what he described as a "national duty", he also promised that the government would investigate allegations that some goods, mostly flats or artworks, confiscated by occupying Nazis or local collaborators from murdered Jews in World War Two were still in government hands.

Many foreign ambassadors were present. Eyes popped when Palestinian envoy Leila Shahid walked over for a long, friendly chat with retired Israeli general and ex-foreign minister Ehud Barak, now visiting France. Barak, a leading Labour Party figure, is widely regarded as a challenger for Netanyahu's job.
